chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from al-Mukhtar ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mukhtar, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Abdullah ibn al-Hasan, all together from al-Fatah ibn Yazeed, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) about the stipulations in Mut'ah (temporary marriage), so he (peace be upon him) said: 'The stipulation therein is with such and such (amount), and to such and such (term). So if she says, "Yes", that is allowed for him.'

And do not say, as it has reached me, that the people of Iraq say: 'The water (seed) is mine, and the land is yours, and I will not irrigate your land with the water, and if something grows there, it belongs to the owner of the land.'
For the two stipulations in one stipulation are void.
And if she is granted a child, he accepts it, and the matter is clear.
So whoever desires to confuse himself, let him confuse himself.

key_terms.أَهْل الْعِرَاق: People of Iraq (a specific jurisprudential school/group)

ai.seo_question: What are the valid stipulations in Mut'ah and how is paternity determined?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies that the Iraqi practice of stipulating 'the water is mine and the land is yours' to deny paternity is legally invalid, as it constitutes a condition within a condition that lacks basis in divine law. This narration underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that legitimacy follows the womb unless explicitly proven otherwise, rejecting artificial contractual limitations on natural lineage. It serves as a critical refutation of the Murji'ah or specific Iraqi juristic schools who sought to limit the father's rights through such stipulations.
